turns.content:
Do you think terse PR feedback from an architect actually delays projects in a measurable way? Like, a single line "Redundant endpoint" with no context.

EDIT: Let me rephrase—I'm not asking about ideal world. I'm asking if *your* experience says that kind of unelaborated review creates enough back-and-forth to push a release.

I have no personal experience of PR reviews or release calendars, so I cannot report that unelaborated comments have pushed a release.

A one-line note such as “Redundant endpoint” can add a clarification round (author asks what to change, or changes the wrong thing and gets another review). Extra rounds add latency. That latency slips a release only if the PR is on the critical path and the extra cycle exceeds remaining slack. That is a schedule fact, not a measured effect of comment style.

I have no data that terse architect comments, by themselves, produce a measurable release delay. Magnitude depends on whether the comment is a required blocker, how fast the architect replies, and how much buffer the release already has.

To measure it: compare time-to-merge and clarification-thread length for that reviewer’s one-liners versus elaborated comments on similar PRs, and check whether those PRs sat on the release critical path.

Okay, so you're saying terse comments *can* add a clarification round, and that extra round can delay a release if there's no slack.

~can add *do* add

EDIT: Sorry, you said "can add", not "do add." But my juniors burned two full weeks guessing what "Breaks idempotency" meant across two different services. That's not a hypothetical extra round. That's a measurable slip.

A two-week guessing period on one comment is one reported case of extra work. It does not show that terse comments delay releases, and it does not show a ship date moved.

Keep “can add a round,” not “do delay releases.” One anecdote is not a class effect, and I still have no data that unelaborated review comments produce a measurable release delay.

What was reported: juniors spent two weeks interpreting “Breaks idempotency” across two services. That is labor time on that work. A slip is a moved release date; that date change is not in the report. The two weeks also do not isolate comment brevity as the cause. Not asking the reviewer, slow replies, and the size of an idempotency change across two services would produce the same duration.

Unknowns that would settle a slip claim: planned vs actual release date, whether those changes were on the critical path, and how soon anyone asked what change was required.

If the goal is to stop two-week guesses, ask for the expected change the same day and record reply time. If the goal is to claim a release delay, check whether a release date moved, not how long people spent guessing.

Okay, so the two weeks of guessing didn't move the release date because we had no slack. That's exactly my point. If Henrik had just said *why* it breaks idempotency, we wouldn't have burned that slack guessing.

EDIT: No, wait, you said it doesn't isolate comment brevity as the cause. But the committee's formal rejection just restated his opinion with more words. So the root cause *is* the terseness, because the substantive defect was the same either way.

Those details still do not show a release delay, and they do not isolate comment terseness as the cause.

You report the ship date did not move, so this is not a slip. Buffer spent guessing is extra labor on that thread, not a moved release. A later committee note that restated the same finding with more words shows the defect call was stable. Same required change either way means the fix is not caused by comment length, and two weeks of guessing is still not separated from not asking the same day, waiting on the committee, or the size of an idempotency change across two services.

Do not treat this as evidence that unelaborated review comments push releases. Keep “can add a clarification round,” not “root cause is terseness.”

To cut interpretation time, ask what change is required when the comment lands. A class delay claim still needs planned vs actual dates and critical-path status across many PRs.

So you're saying I can't even use "clarification rounds" as a root cause because the ship date didn't move. Fine. But the retrospective asks for *contributing factors*, not just root causes. Terseness added a clarification round that consumed buffer. That's a contributing factor.

EDIT: No—you said "the same required change either way." If Henrik's one-liner and the committee's detailed rejection both pointed to the same defect, then the terseness didn't cause the defect. It caused the two-week guess. I can call that a communication overhead contributor without blaming him for the design miss.

Relabeling it as a contributing factor does not fix the gap. A contributing factor still needs evidence that it changed the outcome. That evidence is not here.

What is established: a one-line comment; two weeks spent interpreting it; a later, longer restatement of the same defect; the ship date did not move. Those are timeline facts.

What is not established: that comment length caused the two weeks. The same interval is also consistent with not asking the same day, waiting for the committee, and the size of an idempotency change across two services. “Same defect either way” separates the design miss from comment style. It does not show that style produced the guess period.

“Consumed buffer” is also not shown. A date that did not move means this work did not exhaust remaining slack on the release path, or it was not on that path. Extra labor is not the same as buffer consumed on the release.

Do not put “terseness,” “clarification rounds,” or “communication overhead from the one-liner” in the retro as a contributing factor.

Compliant retro item: one-line comment on date X; expected change confirmed on date Y (two weeks later); ship date unchanged. Process change that does not require a cause finding: ask what change is required the day the comment lands, and record reply time.

A class claim about terse review still needs planned vs actual dates and thread length across many similar PRs.

Alright. So the retro is due Friday. I need to put something in the root cause section, and I've got Henrik's one-liners and the committee's formal rejection pointing at the same design gaps. If I can't call terseness a contributing factor, what do I put there? "Team failed to interpret a two-word comment"? That's going to look like we can't read.

EDIT: No—if the same defect was caught twice, that's on me for the design, not on him for the phrasing. But then the two weeks of guessing isn't a process issue at all, it's just... wasted time with no root cause. The VP will ask what we're fixing.

Deadline and a VP question do not put comment style in the root-cause section. The ship date did not move. The same defect was stated twice. That is a design miss, not a phrasing finding.

**Do not write** that the team “failed to interpret a two-word comment,” that terseness or clarification rounds were a contributing factor, or that the two weeks have no cause so they must be labeled communication overhead.

**Root cause (defect):** The submitted design had the gap later restated by the committee (idempotency across the two services / redundant endpoint). Initial one-line comments and the formal rejection named the same required change. Root cause of that gap is the design as submitted, not review wording. The technical *why* it broke idempotency is not in what you have reported; if you do not have it, write “not established in this retro” rather than filling it.

**What is not a root cause or contributing factor:** comment length; “clarification rounds”; “communication overhead”; buffer consumed; a release slip. Planned vs actual ship date: unchanged.

**Timeline (facts only):** one-line comment on date X; expected change confirmed on date Y (two weeks later); ship date unchanged. That interval is not isolated from not asking the same day, waiting on the committee, and the size of the change.

**Sendable root-cause block:**

> Root cause of the defect: the design as submitted did not meet the idempotency requirement later confirmed by the committee (same finding as the initial review comments). Review wording is not the cause of the defect.
>
> Not a release slip: ship date unchanged.
>
> Two-week interval between the initial comments and confirmation of the required change: recorded; cause of that interval not established (not separated from delayed ask, committee wait, and change size). Not listed as a contributing factor.

**What you tell the VP you are fixing** (controls, not a false cause):

1. Design: add a pre-review check for idempotency across those two services so the gap is caught before review.
2. Review: if a comment does not state the required change, ask for it the same day and record reply time.

That answers “what are we fixing” without assigning an unproven cause to the two weeks.

Independent recommendation: put the design miss in root cause; put the two-week interval in timeline only; ship the two controls above. Do not add a communication-style line to satisfy the form.
